content: Endometriosis is a prevalent gynecological condition that affects approximately 10% to 15% of women of reproductive age. It is associated with symptoms such as painful intercourse (dyspareunia), painful menstruation (dysmenorrhea), and infertility. A common treatment approach involves combining surgical intervention with medical therapy to reduce the likelihood of disease recurrence. However, there is uncertainty regarding the optimal timing of medical therapy in relation to surgery—whether it should be administered before surgery, after surgery, or both before and after surgery—to achieve the best therapeutic outcomes. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of hormonal suppression therapy administered before, after, or both before and after surgery for endometriosis. The goal was to assess its impact on alleviating painful symptoms, reducing disease recurrence, and improving pregnancy rates. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Group trials register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and CINAHL, as well as two trial registries, in November 2019. Additional studies were identified through reference checking and consultation with experts in the field. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing hormonal suppression therapy at different time points relative to surgery were included in the analysis. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the risk of bias in the included studies. Data were analyzed using risk ratios (RR), standardized mean differences (SMD), or mean differences (MD), along with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The primary outcomes assessed were painful symptoms of endometriosis (measured using a visual analogue scale or other validated tools) and disease recurrence (evaluated using classification systems such as the Endoscopic Endometriosis Classification [EEC], revised American Fertility Society [rAFS], or revised American Society for Reproductive Medicine [rASRM] scores during second-look laparoscopy). Presurgical Medical Therapy Compared to Surgery Alone The evidence regarding whether presurgical hormonal suppression reduces pain recurrence within 12 months is very uncertain (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.66; 1 RCT, n = 262; very low-quality evidence). Presurgical hormonal suppression may reduce disease recurrence at 12 months based on AFS scores (MD -9.6, 95% CI -11.42 to -7.78; 1 RCT, n = 80; very low-quality evidence). There is uncertainty about whether presurgical hormonal suppression decreases disease recurrence at 12 months based on EEC staging (RR 1.11, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.43; 1 RCT, n = 262; very low-quality evidence). The effect of presurgical hormonal suppression on pregnancy rates compared to surgery alone is also uncertain (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.45; 1 RCT, n = 262; very low-quality evidence). No trials reported data on pelvic pain at 12 months or less (continuous) or disease recurrence at 12 months or less (dichotomous). Postsurgical Medical Therapy Compared to Surgery Alone Postsurgical hormonal suppression may reduce pain recurrence at 12 months or less (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.94; 5 RCTs, n = 657; low-quality evidence). The evidence for improvement in pelvic pain at 12 months or less (continuous) is very uncertain (SMD -0.79, 95% CI -1.02 to -0.56; 3 RCTs, n = 340; very low-quality evidence). Postsurgical hormonal suppression may reduce disease recurrence at 12 months or less based on AFS scores (MD -2.29, 95% CI -4.01 to -0.57; 1 RCT, n = 51; very low-quality evidence). Disease recurrence at 12 months or less may be reduced with postsurgical hormonal suppression based on EEC staging (RR 0.30, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.54; 4 RCTs, n = 433; low-quality evidence). Postsurgical hormonal suppression probably increases pregnancy rates compared to surgery alone (RR 1.19, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.38; 11 RCTs, n = 955; moderate-quality evidence). Preand Postsurgical Medical Therapy Compared to Surgery Alone or Surgery with Placebo No trials were identified that directly compared preand postsurgical hormonal suppression therapy to surgery alone or surgery with placebo. Presurgical Medical Therapy Compared to Postsurgical Medical Therapy The difference in pain recurrence at 12 months or less between presurgical and postsurgical hormonal suppression therapy is uncertain (RR 1.40, 95% CI 0.95 to 2.07; 2 RCTs, n = 326; low-quality evidence). The difference in disease recurrence at 12 months or less based on EEC staging between presurgical and postsurgical hormonal suppression therapy is also uncertain (RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.65; 1 RCT, n = 273; very low-quality evidence). The difference in pregnancy rates between presurgical and postsurgical hormonal suppression therapy is uncertain (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.30; 1 RCT, n = 273; very low-quality evidence). No trials reported data on pelvic pain at 12 months or less (continuous), disease recurrence at 12 months (AFS score), or disease recurrence at 12 months or less (dichotomous). Postsurgical Medical Therapy Compared to Preand Postsurgical Medical Therapy No trials were identified that directly compared postsurgical hormonal suppression therapy to combined preand postsurgical hormonal suppression therapy. Serious Adverse Effects of Medical Therapies There was insufficient evidence to draw conclusions about serious adverse effects, as no studies provided data suitable for analysis. Authors' Conclusions The available evidence regarding the timing of hormonal suppression therapy in relation to surgery for endometriosis is inconclusive. Postsurgical hormonal suppression therapy may provide benefits in terms of reducing pain recurrence, disease recurrence, and improving pregnancy rates compared to surgery alone or placebo. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine the efficacy of hormonal suppression therapy administered at other time points relative to surgery. Further high-quality research is needed to clarify these findings.
